en: The Sūtra on the Prince Śūraṃgama,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha together with twelve hundred bhikṣus.
Twelve thousand bodhisattvas, upāsakas and upāsikās, the various heavenly kings, Brahmā and Śakra, as well as countless people, spirits, and nāgas, all came together for this assembly.

The crown prince of King Ajātaśatru, named Śuddhoda, accompanied by five hundred sons of ministers and elders from the kingdom, each holding a golden flowered parasol, departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was. Having offered their golden flowered parasols to the Buddha, they withdrew and stood with palms joined; then, bowing their heads to the ground, they paid homage to the Buddha, and having finished, all remained standing with palms joined.
Prince Śuddhodana, the crown prince of King Ajātaśatru, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask about a certain matter; if the Buddha is willing to speak, I shall ask, but if he is not willing, I will not dare to ask."
The Buddha said,
"Ask whatever you wish.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva obtain such upright and handsome features?
For what causes and conditions is he not born from the womb of a woman, but rather manifested by transformation within a lotus flower?
For what causes and conditions is he able to know for himself the events of his past lives?"
"We pray that the Buddha’s great compassion will explain this for us.
The Buddha told the Prince:
"Those who can endure insults and remain free from anger will, in their future lives, be born as beautiful and excellent persons."

If one refrains from lewdness and does not engage in sexual intercourse with women, then when their life is about to end—whether at the age of one year, one month, or seven days—they will, upon being reborn in a future existence, spontaneously know the events of their own past lives throughout countless ages.
The Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva possess the thirty-two marks on his body?
By what causes and conditions are there the eighty secondary characteristics?"
"For what reason do people who behold the Buddha’s body never tire of gazing upon it?
The Buddha told the Prince:

"When I was formerly a bodhisattva, I delighted in giving various kinds of goods to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, teachers, parents, and the common people, providing whatever they came to ask for. By virtue of this, I attained the thirty-two marks."

A bodhisattva should possess a mind of loving-kindness, feeling compassion for the people of the ten directions and even for the smallest crawling insects; viewing them all as one would an only child, desiring that they all be delivered and liberated. It is by means of this that one attains the eighty minor marks of excellence.
"When a bodhisattva looks upon an enemy and his parents with a mind that is perfectly equal and without distinction, for this reason people never tire of beholding the Buddha.
The Prince again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva come to know the profound sutras, wisdom, and the practice of dhāraṇī?"
By what causes and conditions does one know that the mind in samādhi attains tranquility?
By what causes and conditions are all the teachings spoken by the Buddha so excellent and wholesome,
such that all who hear them rejoice and accept them with faith?
The Buddha told the prince:
"A bodhisattva delights in writing, receiving, reciting, and studying; for this reason, he understands the wisdom of the profound sūtras and attains the practice of dhāraṇī.
A bodhisattva always delights in single-mindedness and right intention; for this reason, he attains the peace and stability of samādhi."

"Whatever the Bodhisattva speaks is entirely sincere and without deception; for this reason, all the people he addresses believe and turn toward him, and there are none among those who hear him who do not rejoice.
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying, "By what causes and conditions does the Bodhisattva study the scriptures and hear the Buddha’s words such that all the people believe them?"
"By what causes and conditions does one come to know the teachings of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma?
By what causes and conditions does one practice filial piety, follow the Buddha’s instructions, and refrain from transgression?
The Buddha told the Prince:
“Bodhisattvas, from lifetime to lifetime, are free from flattery and deceit; for this reason, when they study the sutras and hear the Buddha’s words, they understand them all and never forget them.
Bodhisattvas enter into profound sutras without fear or dread; for this reason, upon encountering the sutras and the Vinaya, they immediately understand their ritual laws.
Bodhisattvas, from lifetime to lifetime, revere the Buddha, revere the sutras, revere their teachers, and revere their parents; for this reason, they attain wisdom.”
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions is a bodhisattva born in the presence of a Buddha in every lifetime?
By what causes and conditions does one question the Buddha, praise the sutras, and clearly understand the wisdom within them?”
The Buddha told the prince:
"A bodhisattva, life after life, sees people preaching the sutras and does not interrupt or disrupt them, nor does he revile them; for this reason, he is born in the presence of a Buddha.
A bodhisattva frequently extols the profound sutras; for this reason, he possesses middle-level wisdom."
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions is one not born in an evil realm?
By what causes and conditions is one born in the heavens?"
"For what reasons and conditions does one not crave sensual desires?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"The Bodhisattva, in life after life, has faith in the Buddha, faith in the Sūtras, and faith in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; for this reason, he is not reborn in the eight evil realms."
The Bodhisattva maintains the precepts without deficiency; for this reason, he is reborn in the heavens.
The Bodhisattva knows that the fundamental nature of the sūtras and dharmas is empty; for this reason, he does not crave or lust after desires.
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“By what causes and conditions are the actions of the Bodhisattva’s body, the words of his mouth, and the thoughts of his mind all pure?
By what causes and conditions is Māra unable to find an opportunity against him?”
For what reasons and conditions do you not dare to slander the Buddha?
Do you not dare to slander the sutras?
Do you not dare to slander the Sangha of bhikṣus?
The Buddha told the prince:
"A bodhisattva serves the Buddha, delights in studying the sūtras, and loves the community of bhikṣus; for this reason, they attain purity.
A bodhisattva practices the Path day and night with diligence and without slackening; for this reason, Māra cannot find an opportunity against them."

All that the Bodhisattva speaks is most sincere; for this reason, the multitude does not dare to slander the Buddha, does not dare to slander the sutras and the Way, and does not dare to slander the Sangha of bhikṣus.
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva possess a voice that is fond of being loud, like the voice of Brahmā?
By what causes and conditions are there eight kinds of tones?"
"For what reason is it known that one can respond to all the thoughts of the multitude?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"The Bodhisattva has been sincere and non-deceptive throughout every lifetime; for this reason, his voice is excellent, like the voice of Brahmā."
Throughout successive lifetimes, the Bodhisattva refrains from harsh speech; by virtue of this, he attains the eight kinds of vocal qualities.
Throughout successive lifetimes, the Bodhisattva refrains from divisive speech and false speech; by virtue of this, he is able to respond to all that people think of him.
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does one obtain a long life?
By what causes and conditions does the body become free from disease?"
"For what cause and condition do family members live in harmony and love one another, not allowing others to separate them?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"Because those who do not kill living beings, for that reason, when they are reborn as humans, they become teachers and possess long lifespans."
By not wielding weapons or clubs to strike others, one will consequently be born as a human free from illness;
by seeing people engaged in conflict and delighting in mediating to bring them joy, one will consequently be born as a human whom others cannot alienate.
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva frequently obtain wealth, goods, and rare treasures without losing them?
By what causes and conditions does he not lose his wealth?"
"Are you not robbed or stolen from by others?
By what causes and conditions have you, Venerable One, attained such eminence?
The Buddha told the prince:

"One who does not covet the wealth and property of others will, because of this, be born as a human in a future life and obtain riches and happiness. Being joyful in giving and free from stinginess and greed, because of this, one's wealth and property will not be lost but will increase further.
Seeing others possess wealth, happiness, and money, one’s mind is free from envy and one does not become conceited; because of this, one will be born in a future life with high status and honor."
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions can one obtain the divine eye that sees through all things?
By what causes and conditions can one obtain the divine ear that hears through all things?"
"By what causes and conditions can one know the matters of death and birth among the people of the world?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"Because he delighted in offering lamps before the Buddhas, for this reason, when he was later reborn as a human, he obtained the divine eye with which he sees clearly through all things."
Because he delighted in performing music and dance before Buddhist temples, he was later reborn as a human being and attained the divine ear of far-reaching hearing;
because the Bodhisattva delighted in concentrated mind and entered samādhi to attain dhyāna, he thereby came to know the transformations of death and birth within the world.
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva attain the four bases of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda) for flying?
By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva recollect and know the events of countless kalpas since his previous lives?"
"For what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva obtain the three types of living Buddhas and then enter parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha told the prince:

"The bodhisattva delights in giving; he constantly provides carriages, horses, donkeys, mules, elephants, camels, sandals, and watercraft to the Buddhas, the community of bhikṣus, and the common people. By virtue of this, he attains the four bases of supernormal power for flying."

The Bodhisattva constantly focuses his mind on the Buddhas; by training in samādhi and delighting in practicing and teaching others, he thereby attains the power to recollect events from incalculable kalpas in past lives.

When a bodhisattva attains the path of *avaivartika*, because they maintain mindfulness without further attachment, they are thereby able to sever the root of birth and death; having attained the Buddha-way, they then enter parinirvāṇa.
The Prince spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does a Bodhisattva preside over the governance of a kingdom?
By what causes and conditions does he participate in the assembly of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha?"
"For what cause and condition does this radiance illuminate the ten directions?
The Buddha told the Prince:
"The Bodhisattva originally sought great vows; for this reason, he has already attained a Buddha-land."
The Bodhisattva delights in giving alms to beggars and rejoices in teaching people to practice the six pāramitās; for this reason, he later obtains a community of bhikṣus.
The Bodhisattva delights in using the seven treasures to fashion flower canopies to offer to the Buddha; by means of this, he attains a radiance that shines universally throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha explained these matters in detail for the prince. The prince was filled with joy, and the five hundred sons of the elders were all greatly delighted.
The prince Śūradatta again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that in my future lives, whatever the Buddha has taught may be fully received by me, fully practiced by me, and may all be fulfilled according to my wishes."
The Buddha then laughed heartily, and five-colored light issued from his mouth. The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Listen to what I shall say.

Prince Śuddharakṣa Bodhisattva and the son of the elder, in their previous lives, all made offerings to eighteen billion Buddhas and all practiced the bodhisattva path. During the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara in their previous lives, these five hundred people were all disciples of that Buddha and were taught by me. In a future age, they shall all assemble together; after six hundred million Buddhas, during the single kalpa of the Mahāparinirvāṇa assembly, these five hundred people shall successively become Buddhas, all sharing the same name: Yaśodhara."

When he later attains Buddhahood, his land shall be like that of Amitābha Buddha; it shall also be equal to that of Amitābha at that time, without any difference. The bodhisattvas who come and go within that land, whether traveling on foot or by flight, shall all be like those in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
"If there are people who hear this sutra and believe in it with joy, they shall all be born in the land of Amitābha.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Prince Śūradatta, along with the five hundred sons of elders, the assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, and the devas, humans, spirits, and nāgas, were all greatly rejoiced; they came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Sūtra on the Prince Śuddhārtha (or *Śubhavyūha*)
